questions.stem: FPI total AUM in India (per 2025):
questions.passage_context:
Capital flows in emerging markets like India follow distinct patterns. Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) respond to global liquidity cycles, risk appetite, and relative valuations. When developed-market interest rates fall, capital seeks higher returns in emerging markets; when rates rise, it flees back. India's equity market has experienced substantial FPI inflows over the past two decades — total assets under management by FPIs exceed USD 600 billion as of 2025.

Yet FPI flows are notoriously volatile. The 'taper tantrum' of 2013, when then-Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke hinted at reducing quantitative easing, triggered massive outflows from India and other emerging markets. The rupee weakened sharply, the Sensex dropped, and RBI had to deploy substantial forex reserves to stabilise markets. Lessons learned: dependence on FPI flows creates macroeconomic vulnerability.

Domestic Institutional Investors (DIIs) — mutual funds, insurance companies, pension funds — have grown to provide a stabilising counter-balance. SIP (Systematic Investment Plans) inflows alone exceed ₹20,000 crore monthly. The retail investor base has expanded to over 15 crore demat accounts. This deepening of domestic participation has reduced market dependence on volatile FPI flows.

Going forward, three priorities will shape India's capital markets: deepening corporate bond markets (still thin compared to peers), integrating ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) considerations into mainstream investing, and ensuring that retail participation translates into long-term wealth creation rather than speculative loss. SEBI's regulatory innovations — including ESG disclosure mandates, T+1 settlement, and enhanced retail investor protections — provide the institutional framework. Continued execution will determine whether India achieves its potential as a globally competitive capital market.
